Today they see his first major test at capture the flag and set it beside an ancient K'iche' Maya trial of heroes, the Hero Twins' ballgame.","enduringUnderstanding":"Cultures around the world tell stories of contests and trials to show what they admire in a hero: courage, teamwork, cleverness, and a bond with powerful forces.","futureLessons":"In Lesson 16 students read the Oracle scene in Chapter 9 and analyze what is stated and implied about Percy's future. The evidence and comparing skills from today carry into that lesson and into the Delphi article in the homework.","performanceTask":"The Shared Stories, Shared Lessons task asks students to compare texts, use evidence from more than one source, use abstract nouns, and keep their writing cohesive. Today's paragraph is a short rehearsal of all four."},"vocabulary":[{"word":"identity","definition":"who a person truly is, including their qualities and where they come from","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"transformation","definition":"a big change in how someone or something looks, acts, or is","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"responsibility","definition":"a duty or job that a person is expected to take care of","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"fate","definition":"the events believed to be planned for a person by a power beyond their control","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"trial","definition":"a difficult test of a person's strength, skill, or character","tier":"support"},{"word":"supernatural","definition":"beyond what science can explain, such as gods, spirits, or magic","tier":"support"},{"word":"contest","definition":"a game or competition in which people try to win","tier":"support"},{"word":"outwit","definition":"to beat someone by being smarter or more clever","tier":"support"}],"texts":[{"title":"The Lightning Thief (Chapter 8)","author":"Rick Riordan","pages":"pp. 117–126"},{"title":"Popol Vuh: the Hero Twins' ballgame and the lords of Xibalba (excerpt)","author":"K'iche' Maya sacred narrative, English translation by Lewis Spence (Project Gutenberg)","pages":"Short teacher-selected excerpt"}]},"sections":[{"kind":"launch","title":"Launch","purpose":"Activate what students know about high-stakes games and connect today's comparison to the essential question.","activities":[{"id":"launch-turn-and-talk","title":"When a Game Is More Than a Game","minutes":5,"standards":["RL.6.9"],"routine":"Turn and Talk","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Think of a game, sport, or contest from a story, movie, or your own life where the game showed what someone was really made of. Tell your partner what happened and what it showed about that person."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What can a contest show about a person that everyday life might not?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"It can show if someone stays brave when it gets hard, or if they can work with a team. In my soccer game our goalie got hurt and kept playing, and that showed how tough she is."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Today you will look at two contests from two cultures: Percy's capture-the-flag game in Chapter 8, and the ballgame the Hero Twins play against the lords of Xibalba in the Popol Vuh. Then you will write about what each contest shows about being a hero."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Prep before class: select the myth of the Hero Twins (Hunahpu and Xbalanque) and the lords of Xibalba from the Lewis Spence translation on Project Gutenberg. Print one to two pages that include the twins' ball playing disturbing the lords, at least one trial in the houses of Xibalba (for example the Dark House, where the twins fool the lords with a red macaw feather and fireflies that look like fire), and the final ballgame. Check the sample responses in this lesson against your excerpt and adjust details if it differs."}]}]},{"kind":"literacy-lab","title":"Literacy Lab","purpose":"Teach pronouns in the proper case, then show how verbs and adjectives become abstract nouns that sharpen analysis.","activities":[{"id":"lab-pronoun-case","title":"Pronouns in the Proper Case","minutes":6,"standards":["L.6.1","L.6.1.a"],"routine":"Language Study","blocks":[{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Pronouns change form depending on their job. Subjective pronouns (I, he, she, we, they) do the action. Objective pronouns (me, him, her, us, them) receive the action or follow a preposition. Possessive pronouns (my, his, her, our, their) show ownership. When you compare two characters, you often name both at once, so check the case."},{"type":"directions","text":"Read each model sentence. Decide whether the pronoun is the doer (subjective), the receiver (objective), or shows ownership (possessive). Then fix any pronoun in the wrong case. Sentence 1: Annabeth gave Percy a plan, and him guarded the creek. Sentence 2: Chiron saw the trident above Percy's head and spoke to he. Sentence 3: The twins fooled the lords with their tricks."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"In sentence 1, who is guarding the creek, and what pronoun should do that action?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Percy is doing the guarding, so we need the doer pronoun. It should be the subjective pronoun *he*: 'and he guarded the creek.'"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"In sentence 2, what job is the pronoun doing, and how do we fix it?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"It comes after the word *to*, so it receives the action. It should be the objective pronoun *him*: 'spoke to him.'"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"In sentence 3, what kind of pronoun is *their*, and how do you know?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"It is possessive because it shows the tricks belong to the twins. The sentence is already correct."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Here is a trick for two subjects: take one person out. You would never say 'Him guarded the creek,' so you would not say 'Annabeth and him guarded the creek.' You would say 'Annabeth and he guarded the creek.'"},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Help English learners notice the three jobs pronouns do and practice choosing the correct form aloud before writing (ELD.PI.6.10).","sayAsk":"Say: Point to who does the action. Ask: Who does the action? Who gets the action? Frames: ___ (he/she/they) guarded the creek. Chiron spoke to ___ (him/her/them). That trick was ___ (his/her/their) idea. Have partners say each corrected sentence aloud twice.","watchFor":"If students choose *him* for the doer, then have them remove the second name and reread. If students mix up *their* and *they*, then ask: Does it show ownership or do the action? Success looks like students naming the pronoun's job and correcting one sentence aloud."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: choosing between subjective and objective pronouns","tryThis":"Give a three-column anchor chart (Doer, Receiver, Owner) with example pronouns. Have students try the 'take one person out' test on each sentence before writing."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Have students write one sentence about Percy and Annabeth together and one about the Hero Twins together, using a subjective pronoun in one and an objective pronoun in the other, then label each."}]}]},{"id":"lab-abstract-nouns","title":"From Verbs and Adjectives to Abstract Nouns","minutes":4,"standards":["L.6.6","L.6.3"],"routine":"Word Study","blocks":[{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Strong analytical writers turn actions and describing words into idea words. The adjective *brave* becomes the noun *courage*. The verb *transform* becomes *transformation*. The adjective *responsible* becomes *responsibility*. Notice the endings *-tion*, *-ity*, and *-ness*. These nouns let you name an idea and then explain it. *Identity* and *fate* are also abstract nouns you can use today."},{"type":"directions","text":"With a partner, turn each word into an abstract noun: clever, brave, transform, responsible. Then finish this frame: Percy's trial shows ___ because ___."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Which sounds more like analysis: 'Percy was brave' or 'Percy's courage is tested'? Why?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"'Percy's courage is tested' sounds more like analysis because it names the idea, courage, and then I can explain how it is tested. 'Percy was brave' only describes him."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Expected answers: clever, cleverness; brave, courage (also accept bravery); transform, transformation; responsible, responsibility. Tell students they will use at least one of these nouns in their paragraph."}]}]},{"kind":"learning-in-action","title":"Learning in Action","purpose":"Part A: Cite moments from Chapter 8 to show what Percy's trial reveals about his abilities and identity (RL.6.1). Part B: Cite moments from the Popol Vuh excerpt to show what kind of heroes the twins are (RL.6.1, W.6.9). Part C: Compare the two contests (W.6.9). Part D: Draft a comparison paragraph with evidence from both texts and pronouns in the proper case (W.6.9, L.6.1.a).","activities":[{"id":"lia-percy-evidence","title":"Part A: Percy's Trial at Capture the Flag","minutes":8,"standards":["RL.6.1","RL.6.3"],"routine":"Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief, Chapter 8","pages":"pp. 117–126"},{"type":"directions","text":"Reread pp. 117–126. Annotate three moments: Percy's strategy in the creek, the injury, and the trident appearing above his head. For each, write what happens and what it shows about Percy's abilities or identity."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What happens to Percy at the creek and after he is injured, and what does that show about him?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Percy fights near the creek and gets hurt, but the water heals him and makes him stronger. That shows he has an ability connected to water that he did not know about, which hints at who he really is."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What does the trident appearing above his head tell us, and how do you know?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"It tells us he is a son of Poseidon. The trident shows up right after he proves his power in the fight and the hellhound attack, and the campers and Chiron react like it is a sign from a god."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Push for evidence, not retelling. Have students point to the page for each moment and use the frame 'On page ___, Percy ___, which shows ___.' Keep all evidence within pp. 117–126."},{"type":"pulse-check","standards":["RL.6.1"],"stem":"In Chapter 8, what does the water in the creek help show about Percy?","choices":[{"text":"The water heals and strengthens him, showing a power linked to his true identity.","correct":true,"rationale":"Correct. The water restores Percy during the fight, which leads toward the trident sign that reveals he is a son of Poseidon."},{"text":"The creek is only a place to hide from Clarisse and her team.","correct":false,"rationale":"Percy does use the creek as part of his strategy, but the scene shows the water does more than hide him; it heals and strengthens him."},{"text":"The water shows that Percy is a weak fighter who needs Annabeth to save him.","correct":false,"rationale":"Percy is hurt, but the water gives him power, so the scene reveals an ability, not weakness."},{"text":"The creek shows that camp rules do not allow Percy to use weapons.","correct":false,"rationale":"The text does not say this. The focus is on the water's effect on Percy."}]},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in explaining sequence and cause in the capture-the-flag scene using adverbials of time, place, and cause (ELD.PII.6.5).","sayAsk":"Say: Tell your partner what happened to Percy and where. Frames: At the creek, Percy ___. After the injury, the water ___. Because the trident appeared above his head, everyone ___. Encourage a place phrase (in the creek, above his head) and a cause phrase (because, after).","watchFor":"If students only retell the game, then ask: What does this moment show about Percy? If students give no detail, then point to one paragraph and ask what happens there. Success looks like a sentence with an event, a detail phrase, and an explanation of what it shows."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: choosing which moments matter","tryThis":"Give a three-box organizer (Creek, Injury, Trident). In each box, students write one sentence for what happens and one for what it shows."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask students to explain how the hellhound attack and the trident sign together change what the other campers think of Percy."}]}]},{"id":"lia-twins-evidence","title":"Part B: The Hero Twins' Ballgame","minutes":7,"standards":["RL.6.1","W.6.9"],"routine":"Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"Popol Vuh: the Hero Twins' ballgame and the lords of Xibalba (excerpt, Lewis Spence translation)","pages":"Teacher-selected excerpt"},{"type":"directions","text":"Read the Popol Vuh excerpt. Annotate three moments: how the twins play, a trap or trial they face in Xibalba, and a way they outwit the lords. For each, write what happens and what it shows about what kind of heroes the twins are."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What trials do the Hero Twins face, and how do they handle them?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The lords of Xibalba, who are bothered by the twins' ball playing, send them through dangerous houses. The twins survive by using tricks, like making it look like their torch and cigars are burning, so they are clever, not just strong."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What does the ballgame show about the twins' relationship to powerful forces?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The twins face the lords of the underworld, who are very powerful. The game becomes a test of whether the twins can stand up to the gods of death, and it shows they are connected to that supernatural world."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Tie responses to what your excerpt actually says. Students should paraphrase or briefly quote and name the source as the Popol Vuh. Remind students that this is a sacred story of the K'iche' Maya, so we treat it with respect as a story that carries real meaning for a culture."},{"type":"pulse-check","standards":["RL.6.1"],"stem":"In the Popol Vuh excerpt, how do the Hero Twins mainly succeed against the lords of Xibalba?","choices":[{"text":"They use cleverness and tricks to outwit the lords' traps.","correct":true,"rationale":"Correct. The twins pass the trials by fooling the lords and avoiding traps, which shows cleverness as a hero's strength."},{"text":"They win by being stronger than every lord in a fight.","correct":false,"rationale":"The twins face dangerous trials, but the text shows them winning through tricks, not brute strength."},{"text":"They avoid the lords completely and never enter Xibalba.","correct":false,"rationale":"The twins do enter Xibalba and face the lords' trials, so this is inaccurate."},{"text":"A camp counselor tells them the plan before each trial.","correct":false,"rationale":"This confuses the Popol Vuh with The Lightning Thief. In the excerpt the twins rely on their own cleverness and teamwork."}]},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Help students explain what the twins do and what kind of heroes they are, evaluating the translator's word choices (ELD.PI.6.7).","sayAsk":"Say: Find one word or phrase in the excerpt that shows the lords are dangerous or the twins are clever. Tell your partner why it works. Frames: The word ___ shows that the lords are ___. The twins are ___ because they ___. This detail shows ___.","watchFor":"If students only name events, then ask: What does this show about the twins? If older English blocks understanding, then read the sentence aloud and have students restate it in everyday words. Success looks like a precise word or phrase tied to an explanation of the twins' character."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: understanding the older translation","tryThis":"Read a short passage aloud together, then have students restate each sentence in plain words before annotating. Provide a mini glossary for unfamiliar names."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask students to explain how the twins' trials show teamwork, since they face them as a pair, and compare that to Percy relying on Annabeth's plan."}]}]},{"id":"lia-compare-chart","title":"Part C: Comparing the Two Contests","minutes":5,"standards":["W.6.9","RL.6.9"],"routine":"Think-Pair-Share","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Make a two-column chart: Percy's capture-the-flag trial and the Hero Twins' ballgame. Add rows for: how the contest tests the hero; what it shows about courage, skill, or cleverness; the connection to powerful forces; and how it moves the plot. Write at least one piece of evidence for each text in each row."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What is the same in both stories, and what is different?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"In both, a contest tests the hero and shows a link to powerful beings, like Poseidon or the lords of Xibalba. They are different because Percy wins through a power he just discovered, and the twins win mostly through cleverness and tricks."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"When you write, use words like *both*, *similarly*, *however*, *while*, and *in contrast*. They tell your reader whether you are showing a similarity or a difference."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Give students language for comparing and contrasting with connectors and adverbials (ELD.PII.6.5, ELD.PI.6.10).","sayAsk":"Say: Compare the two trials aloud with your partner before writing. Frames: Both Percy and the Hero Twins ___. Similarly, ___. However, Percy ___ while the twins ___. In contrast, ___.","watchFor":"If students list facts about each story separately, then ask: How are they alike? How are they different? If students overuse *and*, then offer *similarly* and *however*. Success looks like at least one similarity and one difference stated with a connector."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: finding similarities","tryThis":"Ask guiding questions: Who or what tests the hero? What does the hero risk? What powerful force is connected to the hero? Have students answer for each story in the chart."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask students to add a row for the value each culture seems to admire most and support it with evidence from both texts."}]}]},{"id":"lia-draft-paragraph","title":"Part D: Draft a Comparison Paragraph","minutes":10,"standards":["W.6.9","L.6.1","L.6.1.a","W.6.2"],"routine":"Quick Write","blocks":[{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"A comparison paragraph starts with a topic sentence that names both trials and the big idea. Then you give evidence from Percy's trial, evidence from the twins' trial, and compare/contrast words that connect them. End by explaining what each trial shows about being a hero. Use at least one abstract noun, such as courage, cleverness, identity, or responsibility, and check your pronouns."},{"type":"directions","text":"Use your chart to write one paragraph that answers: What does each trial, Percy's capture-the-flag game and the Hero Twins' ballgame, show about being a hero? Include a clear topic sentence, specific evidence from Chapter 8 and from the Popol Vuh, at least two compare/contrast words, at least one abstract noun, and pronouns in the proper case. Underline your compare/contrast words."},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Percy's capture-the-flag trial and the Hero Twins' ballgame both show that a hero's courage is tested by a contest tied to powerful forces. In Chapter 8, Percy is injured in the fight, but the creek heals him, and the trident appears above his head, which reveals his identity as a son of Poseidon. Similarly, the Hero Twins face the lords of Xibalba, who are very powerful, and the trials in their houses test whether the twins can survive. However, Percy succeeds through a power he has just discovered, while the twins succeed through cleverness, like tricking the lords with a fake fire. In contrast to Percy, who still needs help from Annabeth's plan, the twins work together as a pair. Both stories show that heroes prove themselves when they face danger, but each culture also highlights a different strength: Percy's growing identity and the twins' cleverness."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Circulate and confer with students who write two separate summaries. Ask them to move one comparison word into each sentence. Check that every piece of evidence is paraphrased or briefly quoted and names its source. Quick pronoun check: read one sentence with two names and ask students to remove one name to test the case."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"shared","text":"Checklist: a topic sentence naming both trials and a big idea; evidence from The Lightning Thief; evidence from the Popol Vuh; at least two compare/contrast words (both, similarly, however, while, in contrast); at least one abstract noun; pronouns in the proper case; a final sentence explaining what each trial shows about being a hero."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in writing a comparison paragraph with evidence from two texts, connectors, and added detail through adverbials (ELD.PI.6.10, ELD.PII.6.5).","sayAsk":"Say: Tell your partner your topic sentence before you write it. Frames: Both ___ and ___ show that a hero's ___ is tested by ___. In Chapter 8, Percy ___. Similarly, the Hero Twins ___. However, ___ while ___. These trials show that being a hero means ___.","watchFor":"If students copy sentences from the texts, then prompt: Close the book and say the idea in your own words first. If students write only about one text, then ask: Where is your evidence from the other story? Success looks like a paragraph with evidence from both texts, two connectors, and a closing explanation."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: starting the paragraph","tryThis":"Offer this starter: Percy's capture-the-flag trial and the Hero Twins' ballgame both show that ___. Have students rehearse one sentence aloud, write it, then move to the next."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Challenge students to add a sentence explaining which hero's trial reveals more about his culture's values, and to replace a basic word like *showed* with a more precise verb such as *reveals* or *demonstrates*."}]}]}]},{"kind":"look-back","title":"Look Back","purpose":"Students reflect on how comparing two trials helps them understand what makes a hero.","activities":[{"id":"look-back-turn-and-talk","title":"What Do Trials Show?","minutes":5,"standards":["W.6.9","RL.6.9"],"routine":"Turn and Talk","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Share one sentence from your paragraph with a partner. Then discuss the question below."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Why does comparing Percy's trial to the Hero Twins' ballgame help you understand what makes a hero?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Seeing the two stories side by side shows me patterns, like how both heroes are tested by something connected to powerful beings. It also shows differences, like cleverness versus a newly discovered power, which helps me understand what each culture values."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"This comparing and evidence-gathering is exactly what you will do in the Shared Stories, Shared Lessons performance task."}]}]},{"kind":"homework","title":"Homework","purpose":"Optional reading to prepare for Chapter 9 and the Oracle scene.","activities":[{"id":"homework-reading","title":"Chapter 9 and Delphi Reading","minutes":0,"standards":["RL.6.10"],"routine":"Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"1. Read the summary of Chapter 9 (pp. 127 to the middle of p. 139, ending with \"'…we will talk more.'\"). 2. Read and annotate The Lightning Thief Chapter 9 from p. 139 (\"Four flights up,…\") to p. 148. 3. Read and annotate the informational article on Delphi and the Oracle of Apollo. As you read, mark places where a prophecy or a prediction about the future is stated or hinted."}]}]}]},"digest":{"summary":"Students cite evidence from Chapter 8 (pp. 117–126) of The Lightning Thief and from the Popol Vuh story of the Hero Twins' ballgame to compare how each contest tests a hero. They review pronouns in the proper case, practice turning verbs and adjectives into abstract nouns, and write a comparison paragraph with evidence from both texts.","keyActivities":["Turn and Talk on what a game can reveal about a person","Language Study on pronoun case and word study on abstract nouns","Annotating Percy's creek strategy, injury, and trident moment","Annotating the Hero Twins' trials in Xibalba","Two-column comparison chart","Quick Write comparison paragraph with compare/contrast language"],"vocabularyTaught":["identity","transformation","responsibility","fate","trial","supernatural","contest","outwit"],"standardsCovered":["RL.6.1","W.6.9","L.6.1","L.6.1.a","RL.6.3","RL.6.9","W.6.2","L.6.3","L.6.6","RL.6.10"]}}
